hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

assessments.reason: Self-parented Skype app start, no credential access.
PsExec-delivered payload that spawned the harvesting PowerShell, Rar and sdelete.
Password-protected archive of harvested user files, then deleted with sdelete.
Anti-forensics deletion of Rar.exe and staged working.zip archives.
Azure guest-agent log collection, 0x1410 lsass read mask.
Attacker-staged tool run by PowerShell, wrote passwordsDB.
Lateral movement to NASHUA with cleartext pbeesly password.
Anti-forensics deletion of payload and staged archives.
Masqueraded screen-saver dropper from explorer that wrote monkey.png.
PowerShell-driven compile of attacker DLLs in Temp.
Elevated via runas, then ran registry-stored Invoke-Expression payload.
UAC-bypass-capable binary spawned by cmd in attacker session.

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network harvested credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: LSASS memory access or dumping (e.g., procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, Mimikatz), SAM/SECURITY hive or NTDS.dit extraction, credential-store or DPAPI access, Kerberoasting/AS-REP roasting, or suspicious access to lsass.exe by non-standard processes.
frame.what_would_refute: No evidence of credential-dumping tooling, no anomalous lsass.exe access, no registry hive or credential-store extraction, and no Kerberos ticket-request anomalies on the affected hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: SysinternalsSuite (contains procdump) downloaded and extracted by the hidden PowerShell stager on scranton immediately before lsass access; no direct dump-tool command line captured.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: PowerShell 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff lsass handles on scranton and nashua.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: SAM opened with 0xf003f by lsass on scranton after attacker tooling.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow, no .dit file activity, no NTDS object access on any host.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: lsass accessors are baseline svchost/AntimalwareConfig/WindowsAzureTelemetryService; no lsadump or SECURITY hive copy.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: NL$1 writes performed by lsass.exe itself (normal cache refresh); no mscache/dcc2 dumping tooling.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: Single 4662 replication-GUID read by machine account NEWYORK$ on its own object; no user-account DCSync pattern.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is the Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service) invoking Microsoft-signed netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes' as SYSTEM on scranton.dmevals.local for ~7 seconds, plus its own install/start. No pktmon/windump/tcpdump/rawcap command lines, no pcap/npcap/wpcap driver loads, no capture-related PowerShell script blocks and no .pcap/.cap files were found. The genuine attacker activity in the window (PsExec with plaintext credentials to nashua, python.exe beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443) is lateral movement/C2, not network sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Get-Clipboard executed in pbeesly session on scranton.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: Get-Clipboard executed as pbeesly on scranton at 03:06:42Z right after the stager; no SetWindowsHookEx/GetAsyncKeyState keylogger code found, so input capture is clipboard-based.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Only legitimate LogonUI.exe (winlogon parent) and consent.exe (svchost parent) GUI processes; no fake credential-prompt binaries or Get-Credential script blocks.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No web-portal capture artefacts in Windows telemetry; only normal davclnt.dll DavSetCookie WebDAV activity. Zeek window does not overlap.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe (scranton, 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF, UNKNOWN call trace) and wsmprovhost.exe (nashua, 0x1F3FFF) obtained full-access handles to lsass.exe; other high-mask accessors are system processes.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625/4771 events in windows.security; the only authentication-failure-family event was a successful 4776 (Status 0x0) for pbeesly. 'net' command-line hits were svchost.exe -k netsvcs and netsh.exe trace, i.e. benign system processes.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons and no net use/net user/password-bearing guessing command lines; the only hard-coded password was a single static credential in the Invoke-Exfil script on scranton, not repeated guessing.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: powershell.exe PID 2976 on scranton.dmevals.local (hidden, -ep bypass, steganographic monkey.png loader spawned by control.exe) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z with an UNKNOWN call-trace module — LSASS memory access consistent with extracting credential material for offline cracking. No SAM/NTDS hive dump was found.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: TargetUserName stacking over 4625/4771/4648 shows only pbeesly plus machine/DWM/UMFD accounts from 4648 explicit-credential events; no single password tried across many accounts, and no spray tooling in PowerShell script blocks.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed authentications at all (zero 4625/4771); type-3 logons are dominated by machine accounts and 20 pbeesly logons, consistent with normal service/administrative authentication rather than replay of stolen credential lists.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: PowerShell and wsmprovhost full-access lsass handles.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: No forced-authentication activity found. The only WebDAV traffic (10.0.1.4 -> 192.168.0.4, Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/DavClnt) is a client uploading /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z, i.e. exfiltration, not a server coercing the victim's credentials. SMB 5140/5145 and Sysmon port 445/139 connections are all machine-account SYSVOL/IPC$/ADMIN$ traffic and System-process connections to internal hosts (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6, fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429). The only shortcut created (hostui.lnk in StartUp on scranton) is not a UNC/WebDAV lure, and no WebClient/NetworkProvider registry changes were seen.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: Post-exploitation credential access via PowerShell on scranton/nashua.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No access to or exfiltration of browser cookie stores. The 162 sysmon file-create hits matching *Cookies*/*Login Data*/*Web Data* resolve to Windows lastalive*.dat service-state files (svchost.exe) and GroupPolicy DataStore files; the single remaining hit is MicrosoftEdge.exe writing its own DataStore\_TempTestAccess.txt during a normal user Edge session on scranton.dmevals.local. Targeted queries for real cookie stores (INetCookies, Cookies\, cookies.sqlite, Login Data For Account) returned 0 in sysmon, 4663 object access on Cookies/Login Data/Web Data returned 0, 4663 on Edge/Mozilla/Chrome paths returned 0, no process command line referenced browser profile paths, and no PowerShell script block mentioned Cookies/Login Data/sqlite/chrome. Zeek HTTP in its separate window used only WebDAV user agents (Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir, DavClnt) to 192.168.0.4.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: A staged credential-harvesting toolkit (Invoke-Discovery, accesschk passwordsDB, Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-Exfil) ran as pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local, followed by reuse of harvested credentials via PsExec64 to NASHUA.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Nashua PowerShell harvested *pass*/*login*/*admin* files into working.zip.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: hostui.exe ran Invoke-Expression on HKLM Javasoft registry value.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No command lines referencing ConsoleHost_history.txt or other shell history files in sysmon process creation.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine cert keys to .pfx on scranton.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: Only svchost.exe Group Policy client writes of cached gpt.ini were seen; no GPP Preferences files with cpassword were accessed.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: Cert private-key export plus lsass access on scranton.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: User profile/Downloads archives staged and exfiltrated from scranton.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No cmdkey/vaultcmd/Credential Manager or Vault file activity, but PowerShell read lsass memory with full access on scranton; LSASS memory access is the credential-store-adjacent behaviour present.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: Zero hits for password-manager processes, .kdbx/.opvault/.agilekeychain files, process access to password managers, or password-manager strings in PowerShell.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF/0x1f3fff and an UNKNOWN call-trace module at 03:05:16Z during a confirmed hands-on-keyboard intrusion, but no LSA/SecurityProviders registry modification was observed.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: 326 LSASS handle opens are svchost (0x1000), Azure antimalware/telemetry (0x1400) and system processes; lsass image load is Microsoft-signed and valid; no LogonType 9, no 4657 LSA changes, no dcsync/ntds script blocks.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: Only file creation is accesschk.exe writing 'passwordsDB' in the SysinternalsSuite folder; no Notification Packages registry write, no 4657, no non-standard DLL loaded into lsass.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739, no reversible-encryption script blocks or command lines, no matching windows.other messages.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/4730/4662 events and no MFA configuration changes in any dataset.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136/5137/5138/5139/5141 directory-service change events; dsregcmd only loads cryptdll.dll normally.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No 4657/4697 in windows.other and no SecurityProviders/NetworkProvider registry writes in sysmon; LSA registry writes seen are by lsass.exe itself.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: L2 evidence shows one MAC (12:34:56:78:9a:bc) acting as responder for all off-subnet destinations and for the intra-subnet SMB session, plus self-signed-cert notices on intercepted flows - an established AiTM position. The ARP/ROUTE/ipconfig hits were benign Azure guest-agent telemetry.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: All 45 SMB/445 flows from 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6 were delivered by the rogue MAC rather than NASHUA's own NIC, with SAMR/LSAR enumeration and unknown_dce_rpc_auth_type weirds; relay is inferred from L2 evidence, not directly observed.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Single MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is resp_l2_addr for 10.0.0.4, 192.168.0.4 and 192.168.0.5 simultaneously - impossible for a legitimate gateway, indicating ARP cache poisoning.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP traffic (no UDP 67/68), no DHCP server event codes 1341/1342/1020/1063, no DHCP cmdlets in PowerShell, and no rogue DHCP binaries in process creation.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: Kerberos ticket events themselves are normal (28 successful AES256 4769s on newyork, no service-account targets), but the same window contains a confirmed intrusion on scranton.dmevals.local where PowerShell opened lsass.exe with 0x1fffff, i.e. ticket/credential material was exposed to attacker tooling.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) accessed lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16 on scranton.dmevals.local inside a malicious .scr -> cmd -> powershell -> IEX/csc -> sdelete chain; consistent with LSASS ticket/hash harvesting, but no forged TGT, krbtgt dump or anomalous 4768/4769 was observed.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: No 4769 for any user service account, all tickets AES256 with Failure Code 0x0, and no silver/Rubeus/kirbi script blocks; the wsmprovhost lsass access on nashua shows a managed PowerShell call trace with no forged service-ticket use.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No RC4 (0x17) service-ticket requests, no user service-account TGS requests, and no Kerberoasting tooling in PowerShell script blocks.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All 14 4768 AS-REQs (pbeesly and SCRANTON$) used PreAuthType 2 with Status 0x0; no pre-auth-less TGT request and no AS-REP roasting tooling.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential artifacts; all 4624 logons use Kerberos/Negotiate/NTLM with only a User32 type-10, NtLmSsp type-3 and a boot-time type-0 SYSTEM logon as rare values, and rare lsass handle masks belong to csrss/wininit/svchost(sysmain,lsm)/SYSTEM PowerShell with PowerShell management-module call traces.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only cookie activity is rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie to 192.168.0.4/webdav by pbeesly on scranton, matching the Invoke-Exfil WebDAV exfiltration script; this is WebDAV auth for exfil, not cookie forgery, and the sole INetCookies file is a service-profile store.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero SAML/ADFS/token-signing references in PowerShell script blocks, windows.other messages or security object/service events; the only token-related items are a benign SE_GROUP_* attribute helper script and the svchost TokenBroker service.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: 4 planned checks, all with zero hits

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: Certificate private keys exported to .pfx on scranton.

Stack connection destination ports to spot SMB/relay or unusual service traffic in the Zeek window.

args.query: event.action:conn AND (destination.port:5355 OR destination.port:137 OR destination.port:138 OR destination.port:445)

checks.purpose: Look for LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS/SMB traffic that could indicate name-resolution poisoning and SMB relay.

args.query: FROM logs-zeek-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.action == "dns" | KEEP @timestamp, source.ip, destination.ip, dns.question.name, dns.response_code, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Inspect DNS queries/responses for anomalous resolution patterns.

args.query: FROM windows.sysmon METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "22" AND (TO_LOWER(dns.question.name) LIKE "*wpad*" OR TO_LOWER(dns.question.name) LIKE "*isatap*" OR TO_LOWER(dns.question.name) LIKE "*localhost*") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, dns.question.name, win.QueryResults, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Detect suspicious name-resolution queries (WPAD/ISATAP) typical of poisoning setups.
Stack registry modifications to find DNSClient EnableMulticast / policy tampering.
Look for service installation or registry modification events in the other-channel dataset.

args.query: FROM windows.powershell METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*enablemulticast*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*llmnr*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*responder*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*inveigh*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, win.ScriptBlockText, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell disabling multicast name resolution or running poisoning tools.
Stack outbound connection destinations to spot traffic redirected to an unexpected internal host (ARP poisoning effect).

args.query: FROM windows.sysmon METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "22" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, dns.question.name, win.QueryResults, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Inspect DNS query results for answers inconsistent with expected resolution.
Stack registry/object modifications for network configuration tampering.
Look for registry/object modification events in the other-channel dataset.

args.query: FROM windows.powershell METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*arp*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*netsh*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*route add*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, win.ScriptBlockText, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell manipulating ARP/routing/network configuration.
Stack source MAC addresses to spot duplicate/conflicting L2 addresses indicative of ARP spoofing.
Look for DHCP client service events (1341/1342/1020/1063) indicating a rogue DHCP server changed DNS/gateway parameters.
Stack all System/other event codes to see whether any DHCP-related codes exist at all in the window.
Stack logon process names for 4624 to spot unusual authentication sources that could reflect AiTM credential capture.
Stack process creations to spot DHCP/network-configuration tooling (e.g. rogue DHCP server binaries) on hosts.
Search PowerShell script blocks for DHCP server configuration commands used to stand up a rogue DHCP server.
Stack UDP destination ports to see DHCP (67/68) traffic and possible rogue DHCP server flows in the Zeek window.
Stack accounts receiving special privileges (4672) to spot anomalous privileged logons tied to ticket abuse.
Stack logoff accounts (4634) to find rare/anomalous accounts consistent with forged-ticket sessions.
Stack GrantedAccess on lsass.exe process-access events to detect ticket/credential harvesting access masks.
Stack source processes accessing lsass.exe to find non-standard tools harvesting Kerberos material.
Search PowerShell script blocks for Kerberos ticket manipulation tooling.
Search other Windows events for Kerberos/ticket-related messages (e.g. KDC or service errors).

findings.title: Hidden PowerShell stager (control.exe parent) opened lsass.exe with full access and read its memory on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z, user DMEVALS\pbeesly spawned a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell (PID 2976) from the parent 'C:\Windows\System32\control.exe"  /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter' — a classic APT29 stager pattern. The command line decodes a bitmap (C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png) into shellcode and IEXes it. At 03:05:16Z that same PID 2976 opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) with an UNKNOWN call trace, and Security 4656/4663 confirm the handle request and a 0x10 (VM_READ) read of \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe by powershell.exe as pbeesly. This is LSASS memory credential dumping. The same actor then used WinRM to nashua.dmevals.local (wsmprovhost.exe PID 7720, also as pbeesly) which opened lsass with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29Z. Benign lsass accessors in the same window (svchost.exe 0x1000/0x1400, AntimalwareConfig.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, MsMpEng.exe, CollectGuestLogs.exe) are baseline AV/telemetry behaviour and are not part of this finding.

findings.title: Hidden PowerShell stager on scranton decodes a PNG-embedded payload and opens a full-access handle to lsass.exe
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user DMEVALS\pbeesly launched a screen-saver binary C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr (parent explorer.exe, /S) at 02:55:56Z. At 02:58:44Z a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell (PID 2976, parent control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter, IntegrityLevel High) read C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png, extracted a byte array from pixel data and IEX'd the decoded ASCII — a fileless stager. This is attacker input/credential capture tooling, not normal system behaviour.

findings.title: Credential API access to lsass.exe from PowerShell and wsmprovhost with full-access masks
findings.summary: Two non-standard processes obtained full-access handles to lsass.exe: PowerShell.exe PID 2976 on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16Z (0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF, call trace ending in UNKNOWN module) — the same process that ran the hidden PNG-decoding IEX stager — and wsmprovhost.exe PID 7720 on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z (0x1F3FFF, call trace through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, i.e. PowerShell remoting). The remaining high masks (csrss/wininit 0x1FFFFF, svchost 0x101001/0x3000) are normal system accessors. No MiniDump/comsvcs script blocks or lsass strings were found in PowerShell or other logs (C081/C082 zero hits), so the hooking is via direct process-handle access rather than a dump utility.

findings.title: Credential material accessed in memory: steganography-launched PowerShell opened lsass with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe PID 2976 (started 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z by control.exe with '-noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden' decoding a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX-ing it) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice at 03:05:16Z with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff — full-process access masks consistent with reading LSASS memory to extract credential hashes/secrets for offline cracking. The call trace ends in an UNKNOWN module, unlike the benign 0x1000 query-only accesses from powershell.exe PID 3876 at 03:01:03Z. No SAM/NTDS file copies or hive dumps were found (the 'SAM' ObjectName hits are lsass.exe itself opening the SAM object as SCRANTON$, and the only *_hash* file created was _hashlib.pyd in a PyInstaller temp dir), so the cracking-relevant artifact is the in-memory LSASS access rather than an on-disk hive.

findings.title: PowerShell and WinRM host processes opened LSASS with full-access masks on scranton and nashua during a hands-on-keyboard intrusion
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 between 03:05 and 03:09 UTC, two non-standard processes obtained high-privilege handles to lsass.exe: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local requested 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) on nashua.dmevals.local requested 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29 with a call trace through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, i.e. a PowerShell cmdlet reading LSASS. These are the only two PowerShell-family sources among 326 LSASS-access events (the rest are svchost.exe, Azure antimalware/telemetry, wininit, csrss, services). The same user pbeesly on scranton was concurrently running a credential/token-focused PowerShell toolkit from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite (readme.ps1 enumerating SE_GROUP_LOGON_ID token attributes, psversion.ps1 containing an Invoke-Exfil function with hardcoded credentials), accesschk.exe, sdelete64.exe anti-forensics, and PsExec64.exe to \\NASHUA with a cleartext password. This is credential/token material harvesting from LSASS in the course of a broader intrusion. No smartcard, SCardSvr, certificate-provider or MFA-interception artefacts were observed, so the activity is credential access rather than MFA interception specifically.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports every LocalMachine certificate to password-protected .pfx files on scranton
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:04:56 UTC (23:04:56 local) on scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly (SID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107) executed a script block named 'Get-PrivateKeys' (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1). It hardcodes the export password 'saribas' via ConvertTo-SecureString -AsPlainText, enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint into $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx. On scranton as pbeesly, Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine cert keys to .pfx in Downloads, Invoke-Exfil 7z-compressed Downloads to \\192.168.0.4\webdav, then cleanup deleted the artifacts.

AiTM positioning confirmed by L2 redirection; ARP.EXE/ROUTE.EXE/ipconfig hits are Azure guest-agent telemetry (benign)
findings.summary: The adversary-in-the-middle position is established by the L2 evidence: one MAC (12:34:56:78:9a:bc) is the responder for every off-subnet destination and for the intra-subnet SMB session, and two self-signed-certificate notices fired on the intercepted flows. The high-volume hits that looked like network reconnaissance on the Windows side are benign: all 11 ARP.EXE /a, ROUTE.EXE print, ipconfig /all and netsh trace invocations on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:19-03:20Z were spawned by Azure guest/telemetry agents (WaAppAgent.exe, WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, NetworkWatcherAgent.exe) running as SYSTEM, which is normal Azure VM health telemetry. The 4663/4656/4670 object-access hits are dominated by routine registry auditing (Session Manager\Environment, Lsa, Winlogon) and the 4657 hits are WMI Autologger key writes, not DNSClient/EnableMulticast tampering.

findings.title: Single MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc answers as L2 peer for every off-subnet destination (ARP cache poisoning)
findings.summary: In the Zeek window (2020-04-30 00:06-00:45Z) all traffic from the 10.0.1.0/24 hosts to off-subnet addresses is delivered to one responder MAC, 12:34:56:78:9a:bc. That MAC is the resp_l2_addr for 10.0.0.4 (66 flows from 10.0.1.4, 54 from 10.0.1.6), for 192.168.0.4 (376 flows from 10.0.1.6 on 8443, 16 from 10.0.1.4 on 80/445/139) and for 192.168.0.5 (3 flows from 10.0.1.4 on 443/1234). A single L2 address cannot legitimately be the gateway for three different IP subnets, which is the signature of an attacker answering ARP for the gateway/router addresses. The same MAC also appears as the responder on the SMB (445) sessions from 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6, i.e. intra-subnet SMB was also redirected through it. The genuine host MACs are 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 (10.0.1.4), 00:0d:3a:13:e3:69 (10.0.1.6) and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1. Two SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert notices ('self signed certificate') were raised on the flows to 192.168.0.5:443 and 192.168.0.4:8443, consistent with traffic being intercepted by a non-legitimate endpoint. Note the Zeek window does not overlap the Windows telemetry window, so this is a separate observation of the same campaign.

Registry reads of LSA and Winlogon keys by powershell.exe on scranton
findings.summary: Security 4663 key-access events show C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe reading \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa and \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon on scranton.dmevals.local as pbeesly (71 Winlogon and 25 Lsa accesses), starting at 02:56:14 UTC, i.e. in the same session that later ran Get-PrivateKeys/Invoke-Exfil. The bulk of Lsa/Winlogon access on all four hosts is by svchost.exe, lsass.exe, winlogon.exe and WmiPrvSE.exe, which is normal system behaviour; the powershell.exe reads are the outlier. No registry values containing credentials were observed being written or read out, so this is assessed as suspicious rather than confirmed credential theft.
On scranton, sdclt.exe was started three times by cmd.exe in the attacker session at 02:58:42-43, immediately before the csc.exe compile; no credential access by sdclt itself was observed.

No Windows Credential Manager / Vault access observed; lsass access by PowerShell is the only credential-store-relevant hit
findings.summary: No cmdkey, vaultcmd, Credential Manager file writes (\Microsoft\Credentials, \Vault) or 4663 reads of Credential/Vault objects were found (checks C182, C185, C186, C175 returned nothing relevant). The only credential-store-relevant activity is the PowerShell process on scranton.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16Z, which is LSASS memory access rather than Credential Manager API use. Other lsass handles (svchost 0x1000, WindowsAzureTelemetryService 0x1400, csrss/wininit 0x1FFFFF at boot) are normal system behaviour. The nashua wsmprovhost.exe 0x1F3FFF handle at 03:09:29Z carries a PowerShell/System.ni.dll call trace and is consistent with the remote Invoke-Command session pbeesly ran against NASHUA, not a dump.

findings.title: SMB sessions to 10.0.1.6:445 relayed through the same rogue MAC; SMB/RPC used for credential access and lateral movement
findings.summary: All 45 SMB (445) connections in the Zeek window from 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6 carry resp_l2_addr 12:34:56:78:9a:bc, the same MAC that fronts the off-subnet gateways, so the SMB session to NASHUA was not delivered by NASHUA's own NIC (00:0d:3a:13:e3:69). Over those sessions the client performed SMB mapping to \\NEWYORK\IPC$ and \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol and DCE-RPC SAMR/LSAR enumeration (SamrConnect5, SamrEnumerateDomainsInSamServer, SamrLookupNamesInDomain, SamrOpenUser, SamrQueryInformationUser, LsarOpenPolicy2, LsarLookupNames3, LsarEnumerateTrustedDomains) against 10.0.0.4, plus ept_map calls to 10.0.1.6. Zeek also logged 'unknown_dce_rpc_auth_type' weirds on both 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 to 10.0.0.4. On the Windows side (non-overlapping window) the same account pbeesly used PsExec64 with a cleartext password to reach \\NASHUA ADMIN$ and drop C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, and SYSVOL GPO files (gpt.ini, GptTmpl.inf) were read from NEWYORK. The relay/poisoning is confirmed by the L2 evidence; the SMB relay itself is inferred, not directly observed.

findings.title: PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with full access (0x1FFFFF) during a hands-on-keyboard intrusion
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, running as SYSTEM per the event's AccountName) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice within 31 ms at 03:05:16 with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff — full-process access consistent with credential/ticket extraction from LSASS. This is the only PowerShell-to-lsass access in the dataset and it occurs inside a confirmed intrusion chain on the same host: a malicious screen saver C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr launched from explorer.exe by user pbeesly at 02:55:56, which spawned cmd.exe and powershell.exe, followed by archive/collection script blocks, a HKCU Folder\shell\open\command DelegateExecute hijack, an IEX loader decoding a payload from monkey.png, csc.exe compilation, and sdelete64.exe wiping the .scr at 03:02:04. No krbtgt hash dump, golden-ticket creation or forged-TGT use is directly evidenced: the 4769 krbtgt requests on newyork are successful normal TGS requests and no 4768/4769 anomaly (e.g. RC4 0x17, missing pre-auth, unknown accounts) appears. The LSASS access is therefore treated as suspicious credential/ticket harvesting rather than confirmed golden-ticket forgery.

findings.title: Only WebDAV cookie set by davclnt.dll during exfiltration staging; no browser cookie theft/forgery

The only cookie-manipulating process activity is rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav run as pbeesly on scranton at 03:08:50 and 03:10:22-23, which matches the Invoke-Exfil PowerShell function (script block b2b03a9c-43f0-4285-837d-f22d4600b2ae, path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) that maps \\192.168.0.4\webdav with hardcoded credentials and copies OfficeSupplies.7z there. This is WebDAV authentication for exfiltration, not forging of web cookies; no cookie text appears in any PowerShell script block or windows.other message.

findings.title: SAM hive value write by lsass.exe on scranton is normal OS behaviour, not hive theft

The 16962 event about remote SAM access restriction is a default security-descriptor notice. No evidence of SAM dumping.

findings.title: No LSA Secrets extraction; lsass accessors are baseline AV/telemetry
findings.summary: The 326 lsass process-access events are dominated by svchost.exe (289, masks 0x1000/0x1400/0x101001/0x3000 with lsm.dll/sysmain.dll call traces), AntimalwareConfig.exe (15) and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (13) — normal security/telemetry behaviour. No lsadump, reg save of SECURITY\Policy\Secrets, or SECURITY hive file copy was found (C032/C035/C037/C038 zero hits). The only SECURITY-related registry writes are HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 by lsass.exe (see T1003.005). The malicious lsass access is reported under T1003.001.

findings.title: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes are lsass.exe updating the cached-credential store, not extraction

No mscache/dcc2/cache-dumping command line or script was found (C040/C042/C044/C045 produced no malicious hits). Note: the actor's lsass memory read on the same hosts could have captured cached credentials in memory, but that is covered by T1003.001.

findings.title: Azure Network Watcher agent ran netsh packet capture on scranton (legitimate platform telemetry)
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:19:17Z on scranton.dmevals.local, netsh.exe was launched as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM with 'trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' and stopped 7 seconds later with 'netsh trace stop'. The parent process is the Microsoft Azure NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (/service) from C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\, and the netsh binary carries a Microsoft signature hash (SHA256=90F0822D26680C8FFD703A080C876F87695580747A3704C169E39E1A8802EA38). The same agent was also seen installing/starting itself via cmd.exe. This is the Azure Network Watcher packet-capture feature, not adversary sniffing: no pktmon/windump/tcpdump/rawcap command lines, no pcap/npcap/wpcap driver loads, no capture-related PowerShell script blocks, and no .pcap/.cap files were written anywhere in the window.

findings.title: No adversary network-sniffing tooling observed; python.exe on nashua is C2 traffic, not sniffing
findings.summary: Hunting for T1040 across all four datasets found no attacker sniffing. The suspicious activity in the window is instead lateral movement: from scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe launched PsExec64.exe with the plaintext credential '-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe' against \\NASHUA, which installed PSEXESVC and started C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe as pbeesly on nashua.dmevals.local. That python.exe then made 348 outbound TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443 (e.g. source 10.0.1.6:60048), i.e. command-and-control/exfiltration rather than passive capture. No pcap/npcap/wpcap image loads, no pktmon/windump/tcpdump/rawcap command lines, no capture-related PowerShell script blocks, and no .pcap/.cap files were found. The logman.exe executions on scranton are the Azure WaAppAgent stopping its own GAEvents/RTEvents collectors.

findings.title: No fake credential-prompt / GUI input capture observed; LogonUI and consent.exe are legitimate

findings.title: No web portal capture observed in the Windows telemetry
findings.summary: No evidence of web-portal credential capture (no injected browser modules, no fake login pages, no proxy/portal-hooking artefacts) was found in the Windows datasets reviewed. The only web-related activity seen was rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie against http://192.168.0.4/webdav on scranton, which is normal WebDAV cookie handling. Zeek data does not overlap this window, so network-side portal capture cannot be assessed.

findings.title: No brute-force activity observed; only a single successful credential validation (4776) and no 4625 failures
findings.summary: Across windows.security (2020-05-02T02:55:25Z..03:28:09Z) there are zero 4625 failed-logon events and zero 4771 Kerberos pre-auth failures. The only authentication-failure-family event retrieved was a single 4776 credential validation on newyork.dmevals.local for user pbeesly with Status 0x0 (success), i.e. a normal successful NTLM credential check, not a guessing attempt. findings.title: No smartcard, certificate-provider or MFA-interception artefacts; explicit-credential logons are PsExec administration
findings.summary: The MFA-interception-specific indicators were benign or absent. The only registry writes touching Crypto/SCard paths were six default Windows values (Cryptography\Calais SymbolicLinkValue, CertificateTemplateCache timestamps, an SCardSvr.dll MuiCache entry) with no smartcard/MFA configuration change, and windows.other contained no SmartCard/SCardSvr/Certificate messages at all. The single PowerShell script block matching *token* was a token-attribute enumeration helper (Get-AttributesMask), not an MFA/token-theft tool. The 15 event-4648 explicit-credential logons are dominated by pbeesly (9) and are explained by PsExec64.exe -u dmevals\pbeesly against \\NASHUA (PSEXESVC.exe on nashua, TargetServerName NASHUA/localhost), plus routine DWM-1/DWM-2/UMFD-0/UMFD-1/UMFD-2 and SCRANTON$ machine-account logons from winlogon/wininit/taskhostw. Logon types were 3 (218), 5 (61), 2 (15), 10 (2), 0 (1) with no smartcard (type 8) or explicit MFA-related pattern. Zeek kerberos showed 18 success / 7 failure, and the zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window, so no MFA interception can be tied to it.

On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:18 and 00:32:21 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) used the Windows WebDAV client (user agents 'DavClnt' and 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362') against the WebDAV server at 192.168.0.4:80, issuing OPTIONS, PROPFIND, PUT, LOCK, HEAD, PROPPATCH and UNLOCK on /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. The 401 responses are the client being challenged by the server and then authenticating to it; the direction of authentication is client->server, the opposite of T1187 forced authentication (where an attacker lures a victim into authenticating to an attacker-controlled listener). The archive name OfficeSupplies.7z matches the Invoke-Exfil PowerShell function seen on scranton.dmevals.local (Compress-7Zip -ArchiveFileName "$env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z"), so this traffic is best explained as exfiltration over WebDAV rather than credential coercion. No T1187 lure artifacts were found: the only shortcut file created was C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp\hostui.lnk by powershell.exe on scranton (persistence-style, not a UNC/WebDAV lure), and no WebClient/NetworkProvider registry modifications were observed.

The only LSA registry writes retrieved are by lsass.exe itself (LsaPid, LsaCfgFlagsDefault, ProductType) and HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 by lsass.exe on nashua — normal authentication-process behaviour, not network-provider DLL registration.
findings.title: No network provider DLL registration or service installs in windows.other
No DHCP spoofing observed - no DHCP traffic, no DHCP server events, no DHCP tooling
findings.summary: No evidence of rogue DHCP activity. The UDP destination-port stack in the Zeek window contains only 53, 389, 138, 123 and 137 - no ports 67/68, so no DHCP client or server flows were captured. windows.other contains no DHCP-server event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 returned zero hits) and no DHCP-related service installs; the only 7045 service installs are PSEXESVC on nashua (attacker lateral movement, not DHCP) and 'Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service' on scranton. No PowerShell script block referenced DhcpServer cmdlets or 'rogue'. The 4624 logon-process stack is Kerberos/Advapi/User32/NtLmSsp with no anomalous authentication source attributable to DHCP-based redirection.

findings.title: Kerberos ticket activity on newyork DC is normal domain logon traffic; no ticket theft/forgery tooling observed
findings.summary: All 28 4769 events in the window are on newyork.dmevals.local and are ordinary Kerberos service-ticket requests: pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL requesting tickets for krbtgt, NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$ and WEC$ from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6, and SCRANTON$ requesting tickets for NEWYORK$/krbtgt/WEC$/SCRANTON$ at 03:19:13-03:19:58. All have Failure Code 0x0 and encryption type 0x12 (AES256). No 4769 targeted a user service account (query for ServiceName not ending in '$' and not krbtgt returned 0 rows), so there is no Kerberoastable service-ticket burst. The only Kerberos/ticket-related message in windows.other is a single event 6038 NTLM-in-use notice on scranton. No PowerShell script block referenced kerberos/kirbi/ticket/Rubeus/Mimikatz. The lsass access-mask stack is dominated by svchost.exe (289 of 326) with the remainder being Azure agent/telemetry binaries and OS processes; the only unusual accessors are PowerShell.exe on scranton and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua, which are covered in the T1558.001 finding.

findings.title: No silver-ticket indicators: no service-account TGS requests and no service-ticket forgery evidence
findings.summary: No 4769 event in the window requested a ticket for a user service account (filter excluding machine accounts ending in '$' and krbtgt returned 0 rows); all service names are krbtgt, NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$ and WEC$ with AES256 (0x12) and Failure Code 0x0. No PowerShell script block contained silver/Rubeus/kirbi/kerberos strings. The only lsass access by a non-OS binary is PowerShell.exe on scranton (0x1fffff, 03:05:16) and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua (0x1f3fff, 03:09:29); the wsmprovhost call trace is entirely managed PowerShell/System assemblies (Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll), i.e. a WinRM PowerShell session, and no forged service ticket or service-account hash use follows it. Nothing in the data shows a service ticket being forged or replayed.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 service-ticket requests and no roasting tooling
findings.summary: All 28 4769 events carry Ticket Encryption Type 0x12 (AES256) and Failure Code 0x0, and none targets a user service account, so there is no RC4 (0x17) service-ticket request burst characteristic of Kerberoasting. No PowerShell script block matched kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus/GetUserSPNs. The 4769 volume is low (28 events over ~17 minutes) and confined to newyork.dmevals.local, consistent with normal domain logon traffic from pbeesly and the SCRANTON$ machine account.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting: all 14 AS-REQs used pre-authentication
findings.summary: All 14 4768 events on newyork.dmevals.local have PreAuthType 2 (pre-authentication enabled), Status 0x0 and AES256 (0x12) — 8 for pbeesly from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 between 03:11:18 and 03:20:45, and 6 for the SCRANTON$ machine account at 03:19:13-03:19:34. No account requested a TGT without pre-authentication, which is the prerequisite for AS-REP roasting, and no PowerShell script block matched asreproast/GetNPUsers/Rubeus/asrep.

findings.title: No forged web credential activity; lsass handle opens are OS/management components
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) there is no evidence of forged web credentials. All 297 4624 logons use only Kerberos (217), Negotiate (78), NTLM (1) and one '-' package; the rare logon-process values are a User32/Negotiate type-10 logon and an NtLmSsp/NTLM type-3 logon for pbeesly from 172.18.39.2 on scranton, plus a type-0 SYSTEM logon at 03:19:09 during a boot sequence. The rare lsass handle-access masks (0x1fffff, 0x1f3fff, 0x101001, 0x1000000, 0x3000) come from Windows components: csrss.exe and wininit.exe at 03:19:09 on scranton (boot), svchost.exe running sysmain.dll and lsm.dll, and SYSTEM-context PowerShell.exe/wsmprovhost.exe whose call traces resolve into System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll (PowerShell management cmdlets), not credential-dumping code. No ADFS/SAML/cookie objects appear in security object-access or service events.

findings.title: No SAML token forgery or ADFS token-signing access observed
findings.summary: No SAML/ADFS artifacts exist in the collected windows data: zero hits for SAML/ADFS/NotOnOrAfter/token-signing in PowerShell script blocks and windows.other messages, and zero security events referencing ADFS objects, services or processes. The only 'token' PowerShell hit is a benign Get-AttributesMask helper (SE_GROUP_* token attribute constants) in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1 run by pbeesly on scranton at 03:04:04, and the only 'Token' process is svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s TokenBroker (Windows Token Broker service). The high-access lsass opens are SYSTEM PowerShell/wsmprovhost with PowerShell management-module call traces, not token-signing key theft.

incidents.title: SysinternalsSuite staged on scranton ahead of LSASS access
incidents.rationale: Download and extraction of SysinternalsSuite (containing procdump) immediately preceding the lsass access; no dump utility command line observed, so generic OS Credential Dumping.

incidents.title: Steganographic PowerShell stager opens LSASS with full access on scranton
incidents.rationale: All describe the same action: hidden PowerShell PID 2976 (parent control.exe, decoding monkey.png) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff at 03:05:16Z on scranton, plus the wsmprovhost LSASS handle on nashua. LSASS memory access is best fit by T1003.001.

incidents.title: SAM hive opened with 0xf003f by lsass.exe after attacker tooling
incidents.rationale: Five 4656 events show SAM opened with 0xf003f by lsass.exe right after attacker LSASS access and cleanup; Security Account Manager.

incidents.title: Clipboard harvesting via Get-Clipboard in pbeesly session
incidents.rationale: Get-Clipboard executed in the compromised session to harvest copied secrets; input capture, no keylogger code found.

incidents.title: Masqueraded .scr dropper and hidden steganographic PowerShell stager
incidents.rationale: ProgramData screen-saver dropper wrote monkey.png and control.exe launched the hidden stager that drove the credential-theft chain; input capture grouping.

incidents.title: PowerShell-driven csc.exe compiled attacker DLLs in Temp
incidents.rationale: csc.exe invoked by attacker PowerShell to compile DLLs in user Temp; grouped under input capture as the credential-access-adjacent action.

incidents.title: cmd.exe from .scr dropper launched attacker PowerShell chain
incidents.rationale: cmd.exe spawned by the .scr dropper launched the PowerShell chain performing credential theft.

incidents.title: Credential-harvesting toolkit: accesschk passwordsDB, discovery, archive staging
incidents.rationale: accesschk.exe wrote passwordsDB and cleartext pbeesly credentials were reused in PsExec64; credentials in files is the best fit for the collected credential artifacts.

incidents.title: Nashua: PsExec-launched python.exe ran credential-file harvesting and RAR staging
incidents.rationale: PowerShell collected *pass*/*login*/*admin* files into working.zip and password-protected it; credentials in files.

incidents.title: Registry reads of LSA and Winlogon keys by powershell.exe
incidents.rationale: 4663 events show powershell.exe reading LSA and Winlogon registry keys in the attacker session; credentials in registry.

incidents.title: sdclt.exe spawned by cmd.exe in attacker session
incidents.rationale: sdclt.exe started by cmd.exe just before the csc.exe compile; no credential access by sdclt observed, low confidence registry-credential context.

incidents.title: Private-key/certificate export and credential-store theft on scranton
incidents.rationale: Get-PrivateKeys exported every LocalMachine certificate private key to a password-protected .pfx, followed by LSASS access and cleanup; private key theft is the best fit.

incidents.title: User credential-bearing files archived and staged for exfiltration
incidents.rationale: Draft.Zip written and Downloads compressed into OfficeSupplies.7z then deleted; browser credential store theft is the closest in-scope fit for the user credential-file collection.

incidents.title: No Credential Manager/Vault access; LSASS handle is the only store-relevant hit
incidents.rationale: Finding explicitly reports no Credential Manager activity; the only credential-store-relevant event is the LSASS handle, assessed under Windows Credential Manager as the closest in-scope store technique.

incidents.title: Adversary-in-the-middle positioning confirmed by L2 redirection
incidents.rationale: L2 redirection and self-signed cert notices establish AiTM; ARP/ROUTE/ipconfig hits attributed to Azure guest agent are benign.

incidents.title: SMB session to NASHUA relayed through rogue MAC with SAMR/LSAR enumeration
incidents.rationale: SMB 445 flows to 10.0.1.6 delivered via the rogue MAC with DCE-RPC SAMR/LSAR enumeration; name resolution poisoning and SMB relay.

incidents.title: ARP cache poisoning: single MAC fronts all off-subnet destinations
incidents.rationale: One MAC (12:34:56:78:9a:bc) is L2 responder for three different subnets, the signature of ARP cache poisoning.

incidents.title: WebDAV cookie set during exfiltration staging; no browser cookie theft
incidents.rationale: Only cookie activity is davclnt.dll DavSetCookie for WebDAV exfil; no browser cookie theft or forgery observed.
